Armed Conflict & Security
• A Russian double-tap strike on a Ukrainian mall killed 16 and injured about 130; nine people remain missing as rescue efforts continue.
• Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities are forcing Russia to import fuel; Romania said it destroyed an explosive Russian drone boat near an offshore gas platform to protect rig workers.
• Domestic violence incidents elsewhere: two injured in a stabbing at a Canada Sikh temple; one killed in a Swedish school sword attack; a Palestinian teen was shot dead in a West Bank settler attack.
Why it matters: Intensifying strikes and spillover security incidents underline mounting risks to civilians and energy infrastructure well beyond front lines.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39egw7nmk2o https://www.npr.org/2026/08/21/nx-s1-5939990/russia-imports-gas-as-ukrainian-strikes-result-in-shortages https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/08/explosive-russian-drone-boat-destroyed-near-european-offshore-gas-site/ https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8l7w0n0jeo

Economy & Markets
• The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn of Canadian goods after talks failed; Canada vowed dollar-for-dollar retaliation, straining the USMCA framework.
• Bond market tensions and elevated rates loom over growth, with commentary warning policymakers can’t “boss” markets; global pressures include Qatar cutting spending amid Hormuz conflict.
• Big-ticket corporate moves: Broadcom seeks $70–$80bn in debt financing; Samsung plans up to $80bn in shareholder returns; AI listings like Anthropic flag public backlash risks.
Why it matters: Trade ruptures and tighter financial conditions threaten to lift costs and unsettle investment just as capital-intensive tech cycles accelerate.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgvyy4x2mvo https://www.ft.com/content/24f9c08e-e23f-434e-b0f4-fc1eb55a7b04?syn-25a6b1a6=1 https://apnews.com/article/bond-market-yields-treasury-mortgages-savings-b62bedeb7a8b7d5479e25a560b52176c https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/21/broadcom-debt-deal-expected-to-reach-upwards-of-70-billion-sources.html https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/21/-anthropic-ipo-filing-will-show-ai-backlash-as-risk-sources-say.html

Society & Human Rights
• TikTok will pay $400m to settle U.S. child privacy claims alleging unlawful data collection from users under 13.
• A federal judge struck down the administration’s immigrant visa suspension affecting 75 countries; meanwhile USPS moved to tighten mail-in voting rules despite court orders blocking changes.
• Migration and rights pressures endure: at least 13 Tunisians are missing after a boat capsized; Hong Kong’s independent bookshops are closing; Germany has become Europe’s largest regulated cannabis market.
Why it matters: Platform accountability, immigration policy and civil liberties are converging flashpoints shaping public trust and social cohesion.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyr0l45xjro https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/22/us-judge-strikes-down-trump-immigrant-visa-ban-affecting-75-countries https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/21/us-postal-service-mail-in-voter-rule https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/22/at-least-13-tunisians-missing-as-migrant-boat-headed-for-italy-capsizes https://www.ft.com/content/6541cb37-1bc7-4f52-a8ef-f503d13be4ce

Entertainment
• Harry and Meghan return to the UK amid slimmer media deals and questions over their next act; reports suggest Meghan may re-enter acting on a Netflix project.
• Creator platforms and social media face shifts and scrutiny: Patreon will tweak discovery to boost smaller creators; a major case against Meta could redefine Instagram and doomscrolling habits.
• Festivals and releases: Sarajevo’s top prize went to Everytime; Olivia Rodrigo released a Handmaid’s Tale-inspired track; Take-Two subpoenaed Microsoft and Discord in a GTA VI leak probe.
Why it matters: Changing economics and legal frameworks around platforms are reshaping how culture is made, monetized and distributed.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0l5d387j18o https://www.vogue.com/article/meghan-markle-the-gentlemen-uk-acting-return https://www.theverge.com/tech/983156/patreon-update-roadmap-algorithm-changes https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/21/meta-social-media-lawsuit-trial-instagram-facebook.html https://variety.com/2026/film/global/sandra-wollner-everytime-wins-sarajevo-film-festival-1236840695/ https://www.theverge.com/games/983323/grand-theft-auto-vi-gta-leaks-microsoft-discord-subpoenaed

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• U.S.-Canada trade relations deteriorated with new U.S. tariffs; Canada plans retaliation while Mexico seeks softened terms on autos and steel.
• Iran’s president called for ending war with the U.S. from a “position of strength” as Tehran downplays economic pressure; Trump’s outreach to North Korea raises concerns in Seoul.
• Israel is rapidly expanding West Bank settlements; Nigeria’s rift with Sahel states complicates joint security efforts; California leaders push for a Paramount antitrust settlement.
Why it matters: Trade, security and legal decisions are testing alliances and regional stability from North America to the Middle East and West Africa.
Sources: https://www.npr.org/2026/08/22/nx-s1-5941584/us-canada-tariffs https://www.ft.com/content/9a094571-604d-4f1e-b5ff-c0b5dc032dc1 https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2lq5g4dedpo https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/22/nigeria-and-the-sahel-a-growing-security-divide https://www.npr.org/2026/08/21/g-s1-139466/as-trump-courts-kim-pyongyang-ups-price-while-seoul-fears-being-sidelined

Science & Technology
• Space ambitions surge: a new U.S. policy targets 1,000 launches per year by 2030; China’s Chang’e‑7 aims to probe lunar ice; Japan showcased its Mars moon sample-return spacecraft ahead of October launch.
• Tech companies recalibrate: Apple is cutting roles on Vision Pro and Siri teams; Walmart will roll out Apple Pay and Google Pay; Tesla ended Solar Roof and faces a 3 million-vehicle recall in China.
• Novel ideas and risks: planned “space mirrors” could brighten the night sky; researchers tap thunder with fiber optics for seismic imaging; investors back orbital data centers amid launch bottlenecks.
Why it matters: Evolving policies and market bets are redefining access to space and the trajectory of consumer and climate-relevant technologies.

Climate & Environment
• A powerful El Niño is developing, potentially the strongest on record, with heightened UK storm risk and severe Indonesian fire threats; Greenland meltwater may be amplifying European heatwaves.
• Floods and landslides have killed and trapped people in India’s Assam and in Peru; European wildfires are exposing buried WWII ordnance; skepticism greets the new Colorado River management plan.
• Shifting policy and impacts: broad U.S. support for banning glyphosate; climate change could triple wheat prices; UK railways brace for extreme weather; sargassum blankets Caribbean shores.
Why it matters: Intensifying climate shocks are stressing safety, food security and infrastructure, pressing governments to accelerate adaptation and mitigation.
Sources: https://www.newscientist.com/article/2586031-off-the-charts-el-nino-is-already-the-strongest-since-records-began/ https://www.newscientist.com/article/2585659-greenland-meltwater-is-intensifying-european-heatwaves/ https://apnews.com/article/europe-wildfires-climate-bombs-world-war-5390dcf3c92c41ec44c2b0a4d9d80157 https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/22/it-was-a-tsunami-floods-leave-death-trail-in-indias-assam https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/21/colorado-river-water-crisis-plan

Sports
• Arsenal started their Premier League defense with a 3-0 win over Coventry; concerns grow that ticket crackdowns and price hikes are excluding traditional fans.
• The Dodgers walked off the Pirates but lost All-Star Andy Pages to a fractured hand; Toronto’s Vladimir Guerrero Jr. passed concussion tests and is set to return.
• WNBA games in Chicago and LA were halted after items were thrown on court; IndyCar drivers lauded the new downtown Washington, DC course.
Why it matters: Early-season narratives, fan access and event security are shaping competitions and audience engagement across leagues.
Sources: https://apnews.com/article/arsenal-coventry-betis-sociedad-marseille-strasbourg-kaiserslautern-mannheim-eintracht-frankfurt-b54f9ecdd86ff51433d00fb2ddcffe22 https://apnews.com/article/dodgers-andy-pages-hurt-429986ccf7e5bec77461cb9a78e3f202 https://phys.org/news/2026-08-soccer-ticket-crackdowns-price-hikes.html https://apnews.com/article/wnba-sex-toys-921466387c651094c1710cc664b875ff https://apnews.com/article/indycar-freedom-250-trump-68e8169a89502f702958d7d609dc8f20

Health & Pandemic
• Victoria’s Labor government pledged free, walk-in public dental clinics if re-elected, expanding preventive care access.
• Moderna and Merck’s personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced melanoma recurrence in late-stage data; fish-skin grafts accelerated burn healing compared with synthetics.
• A series of large U.S. food recalls over cyclospora and salmonella has raised concerns about supply-chain safety.
Why it matters: Innovations and policy moves could improve outcomes and access, but persistent public health risks demand vigilance.
Sources: https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/aug/22/victoria-labor-free-dental-care-ben-carroll-election-promise https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2026-08-21/moderna-merck-cancer-vax-gives-hope-video https://www.newscientist.com/article/2586000-burns-heal-more-rapidly-after-treatment-with-fish-skin/ https://www.theverge.com/science/983241/food-recalls-bigger-out-of-control

Art & Culture
• “Analog” homes are trending as designers dial back on “smart” saturation; art world figure Kenny Schachter urges less complaining and more doing.
• Vintage photos of Charlotte Rampling and new fiction from MIT Technology Review showcase enduring and experimental storytelling.
Why it matters: Culture is negotiating technology’s role in daily life while revisiting timeless aesthetics and forms.
Sources: https://www.vogue.com/article/analog-homes-trend https://hypebeast.com/2026/8/kenny-schachter-state-of-art-hypeart-spotlight https://www.vogue.com/slideshow/vintage-pictures-of-charlotte-rampling https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/08/21/1141726/mother-tongue-fiction/

Artificial Intelligence
• As AI enters labs and studios, debates intensify over credit and control—from who “owns” AI-designed drugs to Hollywood’s efforts to codify human oversight of AI tools.
• Public pushback grows: LinkedIn’s “AI slop” flag surpassed 1 million clicks; creators face backlash for AI promotions; Meta’s AI glasses raise new privacy alarms.
• Infrastructure and research race ahead: Nvidia expands data-center partnerships and agentic methods; China’s Inner Mongolia emerges as a key AI hub.
Why it matters: The AI era hinges as much on governance, trust and compute as on model quality, shaping adoption and societal impact.

Other
• A wry personal essay about a “technophobic” cat reflects the everyday frictions—and humor—of living with tech at home.
Why it matters: How people feel about technology often starts with intimate, daily experiences.
Sources: https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/981738/my-big-fat-technophobic-cat

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• New estimates pushing human lifespan limits toward two centuries draw interest and skepticism as biogerontologists probe what’s biologically feasible.
• Aging biology insights: TIMP2 protein therapy may recalibrate microglia; microglia may mistakenly eat living neurons in ALS; new histology-based aging clocks emerge.
Why it matters: Unraveling aging mechanisms could yield therapies that extend healthy years and combat neurodegeneration.

Economy & Markets.title: Why the bond market is flexing its muscles, and why everyone needs to care
Economy & Markets.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks to members of the media outside the White House in Washington, Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)2026-08-22T04:01:05Z
                                        NEW YORK (AP) — The bond market is one of the few forces in the world strong enough to get politicians to snap to attention. It also helps dictate how much ordinary people have to pay on their mortgages and car loans, as well as how much they earn from their savings accounts and 401(k) plans.This week rising bond yields forced the U.S. Treasury Department into an unusual intervention and raised the specter of higher borrowing costs putting the brakes on consumer spending, the lifeblood of the economy. It also sparked concerns that investors might finally be thinking twice about financing a seemingly endless flow of government borrowing.Here’s a look at what’s going on and how it affects everyone:First, a reminder of what the bond market isWhen governments and big companies borrow money, they don’t ask a bank for a loan. Instead, they sell IOUs to investors and promise to repay the money with a certain interest rate. If those IOUs are set to be repaid many years from now, they’re called bonds. (IOUs the U.S. government will repay more quickly are more often called bills or notes.)
    
        
    

Investors in the bond market often buy and sell these bonds after they’re issued, and they continue to pay the same interest rate. But if the bond starts to look less attractive, a buyer can get bonds that were earlier worth $100 for less than that. Such a drop in price means the new buyer will get a bigger return, percentage-wise, on their money than the interest rate the bond pays on its face value. Those payments are called the bond’s yield.


    
        




    


The U.S. bond market is the biggest but investors have other optionsThe world’s biggest and most important bond market is for IOUs from the U.S. government, which are called Treasurys. The total size of it was $31.5 trillion, as of July, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. Yet Treasurys are facing more competition from higher-yielding bonds overseas than in recent decades. After years of near-zero interest rates, even 30-year Japanese government bonds are now paying more than 4%. Yields on U.K. bonds have reached 5.81%, and German bonds are also paying 3.76%, versus 5.27% for a comparable U.S. bond. It’s a big reason U.S. rates have been drifting higher.Ira Jersey, chief U.S. interest rate strategist at Bloomberg Intelligence, said that large global investors such as pension funds and life insurers used to have little choice to invest in Treasurys because most other overseas bonds paid so little interest. “Now the U.S. 30-year yield has to compete with all these other sovereign bonds,” Jersey said. “The U.S. is not the only game in town anymore.” 
    
        
            
                
                    
    
    


    

  

  
    Read More 
  
  

    
    
    
  

    
        
    

                
            
        
    
The U.S. government bond market helps set interest rates that affect regular peopleThe easiest example is mortgage rates. Rates for these loan tend to follow the path of yields for Treasurys that will get repaid in 10 years. The 10-year Treasury yield is the centerpiece of the bond market, and it shot higher through the summer after the war with Iran sent oil prices higher and worries about inflation upward, adding to longstanding concerns about the size of the U.S. government’s debt. 
    
        
    

That in turn made mortgages more expensive for people looking to buy a house. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is near its highest level in a year, discouraging people already worried the price of homeownership may be too high.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement Wednesday that the government would double its buybacks of longer-term bonds was intended to bring down the 10-year Treasury yield and lower mortgages. Yet the move brought only temporary relief, with the 10-year yield rising back to 4.74% Friday, matching its highest point in more than a year.

Thierry Wizman, global rates strategist at Macquarie Group, said higher mortgage rates will likely discourage some consumers from buying homes. At the same time, higher yields generally should draw more investment into bonds issued by large tech firms investing in AI infrastructure. 
    
        
    

“The private sector wants to have the AI revolution,” Wizman said. “Who’s going to take a step back? It’s going to be the consumer. And higher yields are going to do that a little bit.”Other parts of the market, including where the Federal Reserve sets its interest rate for very short-term overnight loans, affect rates for everything from credit cards to savings accounts to auto loans. Generally, higher yields and rates benefit people who are savers. It means they are earning more from lending money to the U.S. government or sticking their cash in a high-yield savings account. Higher yields and rates, meanwhile, tend to hurt people who are borrowing money. They also drag on prices for stocks, gold and even cryptocurrencies. The thought is: Why should anyone pay high prices for riskier investments when U.S. Treasurys, which are supposed to be safer, are paying more than before? 
    
        
    

Higher yields mean U.S. taxpayers will have to pay more for their government’s billsWashington continues to spend far more than it brings in through revenue, so it has to borrow money to cover the gap. That has sent its total debt over $40 trillion, a staggering record, and the number keeps climbing by the day. When yields are rising, the U.S. government has to pay higher interest rates to entice buyers for its bonds when it auctions off Treasurys. The federal government has already paid $931 billion in interest on its debt through the first 10 months of its fiscal year, which ends in September. That’s more than it spent on health, national defense or veterans benefits and is just behind Social Security and Medicare.
    
        
    

Concerns have been brewing in the bond market for a long timeIt’s no secret that the U.S. government has a lot of debt. Officials at the Federal Reserve, economists, investors and many other voices have been saying for years that the U.S. government is on an unsustainable path with how much it spends versus what it brings in. Everything from tax cuts to increased military budgets adds to the deficit. The unknown has always been when or if a tipping point would arrive that turns the worries about the U.S. government’s debt into a panic. That would cause investors to quickly dump their Treasurys, which would sent yields surging. And while yields have climbed this summer, they haven’t done so at such a pace to suggest a tipping point is here. The climb in yields for government bonds has also been worldwide. It’s not just Washington feeling pressure but also bond markets in Japan, France, Germany and elsewhere.Importantly, a measure in the bond market that shows how worried bond investors are about potential defaults by several big economies’ governments on their bonds has not risen excessively, according to strategists at Macquarie. __Rugaber reported from Washington.

Entertainment.title: Monterey Car Week Is a Five-Day Extravaganza of Automotive Aspiration
Entertainment.text: Monterey Car Week just concluded last weekend, and we learned quite a lot for this year's iteration. Each year, droves of car enthusiasts flock to Northern California for the annual Monterey Car Week held across the namesake town, as well as the neighboring town of Carmel, to witness the absolute best of the best in car culture. The range of automobiles that arrive are inherently wide, varying from niche tuner builds and modern classics to ultra-rare hypercars and historic racers. Because of this, this draws in an exceptionally broad range of enthusiasts, some of whom may be there for all the wrong reasons.Ever since the conclusion of COVID-19, Monterey Car Week (which resumed in 2022 after the pandemic) gradually saw the attendance of car community individuals who were undeniably enthusiastic about the culture, but may not have fully grasped the atmosphere within Monterey and Carmel: wealthy, quiet, traditional, conservative. The population is low and their values are apparent in the town's settings, with the previous years's MCW iterations causing quite a bit of disruption to the serenity and sanity of the quaint countryside. Without going into too far into the nitty gritty of past instances, this year was noticeably more tame, with police, local security, and sanctioned organizers banding together to learn from the mistakes of 2025 and prior.This being our fourth consecutive year as an invited media, we've come to the realization that Monterey Car Week is well divided, with events catering to a variety of car enthusiasts. It's not a case of "there's something for everyone;" quite opposite, in fact. Most of the events are private, invite only, highly exclusive and notoriously strict on guests.  View this post on InstagramA post shared by HYPEBEAST (@hypebeast)The QuailThere are events before it, but in our opinion The Quail serves as the gateway into the week. Held annually at The Quail lodge, the grassy grounds are converted into a trade show of sorts, with exclusive booths for key automakers. This year, BMW ALPINA, Gunther Werks, BRABUS, Lamborghini, Acura and Koenigsegg commanded extra large audiences with their buildouts, each taking their space to show off new cars and concepts. The primary audience for the Quail remains to be media: journalists, writers, reviewers and content creators rush the booths, hoping to get their first glimpse and ultimately share it with their followers. It remains the most purposeful event of the week, and its ultra-steep price tag of $2,000+ USD assures it'll stay that way.HousesScattered throughout the week and county are automaker "houses" that serve as home base for car brands throughout the week. To get invited into the house would be a private invitation to understand the brand, view new products, speak with key figures within the company and more. After those initiatives, the automaker tends to also throw parties, again via curated guest lists. If you're fortunate to attend any of the brand's houses, expect hospitality like no other. This year we were privy to attend the BMW house, alongside Lamborghini's and Bentley's via private invite. Kith x BMW's presence was upscale and sophisticated, while Lamborghini's was impressive in grandeur and activations. Bentley's – as like its previous years – is fun, fun, fun. Think The Great Gatsby with a live band playing Blink-182 songs. Memorable to say the least.Rolex Monterey Motorsports ReunionFor the true petrolheads, Rolex Monterey Motorsports Reunion is the event they dream of. Classic racers, Le Mans legends, IMSA-prepped track cars and much more all hit the legendary Laguna Seca race track for competitive heats, with the general public present to hear, see and smell everything. Attendance to Motorsports Reunion also allows for a general access to paddocks where you can see these cars up close, learn about their histories (and even their previous owners), and truly take in all of what makes motorsport enthusiasts so passionate. If we were to encapsulate RMMU in one word, it'd be "education." Pebble Beach Concours d'EleganceLast but certainly not least is Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance, which is the summit event of the week. Each year, thousands of people attend it to witness how the elite celebrate cars and car culture – via money. There's barely anything on the Pebble Beach launch that's under $1M USD, but if there is, it's certain worth more now that it's officially made it to Concours d'Elegance. Thankfully the tickets are much more affordable than The Quail, but even at $600 USD, it's a bit of a teeth clench. Within Cd'E however are opportunities to witness the awards ceremony, some fine dining, promotional giveaways from auto brands, and even shopping. If you ever have the opportunity to visit Monterey Car Week, and want to truly understand what it is to be "into cars," try to find your way into these events either as +1s, invited media, or ticket holders. Sure, the free street events and car meets throughout the week spell out car culture as well, but we think it takes more than just a pretty paint job and a nice hard park on Ocean Ave. to really understand car culture. Just remember to be respectful, and don't give the cops the satisfaction of pulling over another car.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Climate & Environment.title: European wildfires reveal a hidden danger: buried bombs and mines from WWI and WWII
Climate & Environment.text:
Members of a bomb disposal unit, Dieter Schwaetzler, left, and Rene Bennert sit next to 1.8 ton World War II bomb after defusing it in Frankfurt, Germany, Sept. 3, 2017. (AP Photo/Michael Probst, File)2026-08-22T06:09:44Z
                                        ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944.Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
    
        
    

This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group.


    
        




    


Flames chewed up old battlefields and set off buried explosivesAs they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition.
    
        
            
                
                    
    
    


    

  

  
    Read More 
  
  

    
    
    
  

    
        
    

                
            
        
    
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
    
        
    

“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.

The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops.
    
        
    

Every year, Belgium responds to thousands of calls about explosivesCollard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton.“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” Collard said.Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany.The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest ” because it turns up so many war remnants.Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars.
    
        
    

Flames are not the only threatDrought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water.As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb.Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.
    
        
    

“It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places.”___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report.

Sports.title: Tommy Edman delivers a 10th-inning walk-off single as the Dodgers edge the Pirates 5-4
Sports.text:
Los Angeles Dodgers' Max Muncy, right, hits a two-run home run as Pittsburgh Pirates catcher Rafael Flores Jr. watches during the first inning of a baseball game Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill)2026-08-22T05:47:18Z
                                        LOS ANGELES (AP) — Tommy Edman singled in the winning run with two outs in the 10th inning, lifting the Los Angeles Dodgers over the Pittsburgh Pirates 5-4 on Friday night.Edman hit a line drive to left field off Gregory Soto (5-4), scoring automatic runner Kiké Hernández from third, keeping the Dodgers as the only undefeated team in extra innings in the majors this season.With Hernández starting at second, pinch-hitter Alex Call struck out and Mookie Betts was intentionally walked. Kyle Tucker grounded into a fielder’s choice to second, where Betts was out.Evan Phillips (1-2) got the win with one inning of relief.The NL West-leading Dodgers have won eight of their last 11.Pittsburgh’s Oneil Cruz hit a two-run homer off reliever Kyle Hurt in the eighth to make it 4-4.Betts hit a two-run single with two outs in the third to make it 4-2.
    
        
    

Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed two runs and five hits in 6 1/3 innings with nine strikeouts.The Japanese right-hander was lifted after putting the tying runs aboard in the seventh. Jake Mangum had a leadoff double and Yamamoto hit Jared Triolo. Reliever Brock Stewart came on to retire the next two batters and end the inning.Pirates reliever Luke Bachar set up the struggling Tucker for a potential Hollywood ending in the bottom of the seventh. Shohei Ohtani drew a leadoff walk and stole second. Two outs later, Bachar issued back-to-back walks to Max Muncy and Betts to load the bases and bring up Tucker. However, he flied out to center to end the threat.


    
        




    


Muncy’s two-run, two-out homer in the first gave the Dodgers to a 2-1 lead.The Pirates led 1-0 on Nick Gonzales’ RBI single to center in the top of the inning. He tied the game 2-2 with an RBI single to center in the third.

Sports.title: Dodgers’ Andy Pages fractures hand on hit by pitch vs the Pirates
Sports.text:
Los Angeles Dodgers' Andy Pages is hit in the hand by a pitch during the third inning of a baseball game against the Pittsburgh Pirates, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill)2026-08-22T03:43:45Z

He advanced to third before the inning ended. Pages was replaced by Kiké Hernández to start the fifth.Manager Dave Roberts said X-rays revealed the break. “It’s not season-ending because obviously things like that it’s four or five weeks,” Roberts said. “I would expect him back, knowing him, on the earlier side. There’s still time in the season for him to be back. I feel for him because he’s having such a good year.”Roberts said it’s possible Pages could need surgery, but he doesn’t believe that would change the timetable for him to return.Roberts said utility player Tommy Edman, who had the winning single in the 10th inning, could play some center in Pages’ absence. Pages is hitting .272 with 25 home runs and 80 RBIs. He earned his first All-Star selection this season. ___See AP’s full MLB coverage here

Sports.title: Arsenal, Marseille and Real Betis begin league campaigns with wins and clean sheets
Sports.text:
Arsenal's Riccardo Calafiori leaps over Coventry City's goalkeeper Carl Rushworth during the English Premier League soccer match between Arsenal and Coventry City in London, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)2026-08-21T22:31:34Z
                                        MADRID (AP) — Arsenal got its title defense off to a perfect start Friday with a 3-0 win over newly promoted Coventry City in the opening match of the Premier League.In France, a second-half double from Amine Gouiri set Marseille on its way to a 4-0 victory over Strasbourg on the first night of this season’s Ligue 1 action.Elsewhere in Europe, Real Betis beat Real Sociedad 1-0 in the Spanish league while fan trouble overshadowed the first round of the German Cup.Arsenal sweeps Coventry aside in Premier League opener Newcomer Christos Tzolis helped set up two goals as defending champion Arsenal opened the Premier League season by dismantling promoted Coventry 3-0 to spoil the visitor’s long-awaited return to the top flight.After ending a 22-year wait for the Premier League title, Arsenal showed why it’s favored to repeat as champion by completely dominating Frank Lampard’s side in a game that was one-sided from start to finish.
    
        
    

Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard scored for the Gunners, who spurned chances to pad the scoreline even further.For Coventry, it was a rude welcome back to the Premier League after a 25-year absence. Having won the second-tier Championship last season by a wide margin, Lampard’s side simply looked outmatched as it was repeatedly taken apart by the marauding Gunners.


    
        




    


Gouiri leads Marseille to dominant win over StrasbourgGouiri, who scored eight goals in 22 league matches last season, has been linked with a move to Everton in recent days, but the speculation clearly did not hinder his concentration in the Ligue 1 opener.He slotted home from close range a minute after the break and then doubled his tally from the penalty spot midway through the second half, just minutes after Strasbourg was reduced to 10 men following Samir El Mourabet’s dismissal for a bad tackle.Keyliane Abdallah added a third in the 89th minute before Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg completed the scoring in stoppage time to give new Marseille coach Bruno Génésio the perfect start to the season.

Rowdy fans and startling scoreline in the German CupPolice had to intervene in the German Cup match between Waldhof Mannheim and Kaiserslautern as fans threw flares and other objects and some Mannheim supporters invaded the pitch. The trouble started as the game was heading into extra time with the score tied at 0-0.The match was halted for nearly 30 minutes as officers in riot gear and mounted police pushed fans back into the stands before the players could return.Ibrahim Kanate scored in the last minute of extra time, giving second-division Kaiserslautern a 1-0 win to advance to the second round.Eintracht Frankfurt cruised into the second round of the competition with a staggering 11-0 win away at fifth-tier St. Tönis. Ten of the goals came before half time, three of them from Jonathan Burkardt.Karlsruhe beat Munster 2-1 and Dženan Pejčinović scored a hattrick as VfB Stuttgart beat Hansa Rostock 4-0 away from home.

Sports.title: Blue Jays slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr. passes final concussion tests, expected to return Saturday
Sports.text:
Toronto Blue Jays Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (27) grimaces as he crosses the plate after scoring following a throwing error by New York Yankees first baseman Luis García Jr. (26) during the first inning of a baseball game in Toronto, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press via AP)2026-08-21T22:32:05Z
                                        NEW YORK (AP) — Vladimir Guerrero Jr. passed his final concussion tests and the Toronto Blue Jays slugger is expected to return from the seven-day injured list on Saturday.Guerrero returned to the team on Friday and took swings in the batting cage after doubling during a minor league rehabilitation game for Single-A Dunedin on Thursday.“He felt good,” manager John Schneider said before the Blue Jays opened a three-game series with the Yankees. “Even before he left to play in Clearwater, he was feeling good. He feels pretty normal, so that’s a good thing.”Guerrero left a 3-1 win in Toronto over the Yankees last Friday after a collision with New York rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. on a bizarre play at third base in the sixth inning.The six-time All-Star was injured when he slid at third base and had Lombard’s knee and thigh strike his head. The play caused Guerrero’s helmet to get dislodged, though the first baseman scored the tying run before exiting.Guerrero is batting .263 with seven homers and 46 RBIs. Before the collision, he was hitting .310 (7 for 29) in his last seven games.
    
        
    

Blue Jays make four roster movesNewly acquired infielder Josh Smith was placed on the 10-day injured list with left hamstring inflammation. Smith was injured during Wednesday’s 7-6 loss at Tampa Bay and completed the game.Smith is hitting .250 in 14 games since being acquired from Texas at the Aug. 3 trade deadline.The Blue Jays also activated pitcher Spencer Arrighetti from the injured list after the right-hander missed time with an irritated right foot. Arrighetti was acquired at the deadline from Houston for outfielder Daulton Varsho and was expected to serve as a bulk reliever after opener Mason Fluharty.Toronto also recalled outfielder Davis Schneider, who is hitting .142 with three homers and 12 RBIs in 61 games. Schneider was hitting .219 with six homers and 21 RBIs in 37 games with Triple-A Buffalo.


    
        




    


Toronto’s final move was optioning reliever Brendan Cellucci to Triple-A. The lefty did not appear in a game after being recalled on Wednesday.—See AP’s full MLB coverage here

Sports.title: NHL referee Garrett Rank wins his 4th Canadian Men’s Mid-Amateur golf title
Sports.text:
Fans watch from a general view at Chase Center during the first half of a WNBA basketball game between the Golden State Valkyries and the Dallas Wings in San Francisco, Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)2026-08-21T23:24:37Z
                                        BRANTFORD, Ontario (AP) — NHL referee Garrett Rank won his fourth Canadian Men’s Mid-Amateur Championship on Friday, breaking a last-hole tie with a 6-foot par putt at Brantford Golf & Country Club.The 38-year-old Rank, from Waterloo about 40 miles north, closed with a 3-under 69 for a one-stroke victory. He finished at 18-under 270. Third-round leader Evan Nachtigall of Brandon, Manitoba, bogeyed the last for a 72 to drop into second.“As soon as I saw my ball was on the back of the green, I knew it was a good time for lag putt to try and two putt, and luckily enough I was able to make the 6-footer at the end to win,” said Rank, who worked his first Stanley Cup Finals as a referee this year.Rank’s previous Canadian Men’s Mid-Am wins came three years in a row from 2014-16. He has five national titles, also winning the 2012 Canadian College/University Individual Championship.
    
        
    

“It’s a huge honor,” Rank said. “Winning a golf tournament is never easy. To do it four times is pretty special. I think it’s been 10 years since I last did it so to do it close to home in a place like Brantford is something that I will remember for the rest of my life.”Rank received a spot into the U.S. Mid-Amateur Championship at Sand Valley Resort in Nekoosa, Wisconsin, in late September and early October.___See AP’s full NHL coverage here___See AP’s full golf coverage here

Sports.title: NBA’s 2026-27 schedule gives Jaylen Brown and Giannis Antetokounmpo homecoming games in January
Sports.text:
Giannis Antetokounmpo speaks during a news conference where he was introduced as a new member of the Miami Heat team Thursday, July 16, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Marta Lavandier)2026-08-13T19:18:03Z
                                        NEW YORK (AP) — Jaylen Brown and Giannis Antetokounmpo will play homecoming games a week apart in January.The 2026-27 NBA schedule was released Thursday, setting the dates for the two former NBA Finals MVPs to return to face the teams that traded them this summer.The schedules for opening night and Christmas had already been unveiled earlier this week, so those two games were among the most intriguing matchups not yet known. Brown, who was dealt from the Celtics to the rival Philadelphia 76ers in a stunning move, will play his first game back in Boston on Jan. 21.Antetokounmpo was expected to be traded by Milwaukee this offseason — at one point speculation was that he might be swapped for Brown — and was eventually dealt to Miami. The Heat will travel to face the Bucks for the first time on Jan. 28.Both of those games, which will be on Thursday nights, will stream on Prime Video.Other details about the schedule:
    
        
    

From start to finishThe season will open Oct. 20 with a tripleheader, highlighted by LeBron James, Brown and the 76ers visiting the Knicks, who will receive their rings after winning the franchise’s first championship since 1973.The regular season ends April 11. All-Star weekend is set for Feb. 19-21 in Phoenix. 


    
        




    


Busy nights and nights offEvery team will play on Monday, Nov. 2, and there will then be no games the following night, which is Election Day in the U.S. The league is leaving that first Tuesday in November as an open day in hopes that fans and members of the NBA community will participate in the voting process.No teams will play on Saturday, April 10, the second-to-last day of the regular season. Every team is then in action on the final day, with all the games matching Eastern Conference teams and the one interconference matchup scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. EDT. The games involving West teams are set for 8:30 p.m.
    
        
            
                
                    
    
    


    

  

  
    Read More 
  
  

    
    
    
  

    
        
    

                
            
        
    
Where to watch the gamesThere will be 90 regular-season games televised nationally on ABC or NBC, up from 79 last season. Every team will be scheduled to appear on national TV at least twice. Throughout the season, games will stream on Peacock on Monday nights, be shown on NBC and Peacock on Tuesdays, be televised by ESPN on Wednesdays, and stream on Prime Video on Fridays. 
    
        
    

Saturday night primetime games on ABC begin Dec. 12 with the Knicks visiting the Heat, while NBC’s “Sunday Night Basketball” returns Jan. 24 with Oklahoma City visiting Golden State.Prime Video will begin streaming Thursday night doubleheaders in January and some Saturday afternoon games starting Feb. 6 with Portland at Memphis, when Ja Morant returns to face the Grizzlies for the first time.A lot of TV timeThe NBA champion Knicks have the most appearances on ABC with six, while the Lakers, 76ers, San Antonio Spurs and Minnesota Timberwolves all are featured on ESPN eight times.The Knicks, Spurs, 76ers, Thunder, Warriors, Nuggets, Lakers and Houston all get the maximum 11 appearances on NBC. 
    
        
    

Back-to-backs and schedule breaksTeams will average 14.2 back-to-backs this season, the lowest total since the NBA Cup was added to the schedule, and no team will have more than 16. No team will play eight games in 12 nights, or 18 in 30.There are 59 back-to-backs involving at least 750 miles of travel, down from 74 last season.No team will be scheduled to play the night before games in the NBA Cup, or if they are in nationally televised games on Christmas Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents Day, Sunday nights on NBC or Saturday nights on ABC. Milestone momentsIf Kevin Durant averages 26 points, as he did in his first season in Houston, he could move past Kobe Bryant into fourth place on the career scoring list sometime around Jan. 16, when the Rockets would be at the midpoint of their schedule.Rick Carlisle is set to become the eighth man to coach 2,000 NBA games on March 8, when the Indiana Pacers play their 65th game of the season.___See AP’s full NBA coverage here

Sports.title: IndyCar drivers amazed at downtown DC course: ‘It’s stuff that you dream of’
Sports.text:
Racing teams walk the track before Sunday's Freedom 250 Grand Prix auto race, seen Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)2026-08-21T20:44:09Z
                                        WASHINGTON (AP) — Even for well-traveled IndyCar drivers, a track with the U.S. Capitol in the background is a little awe inspiring.“We get to race at a lot of cool cities, but this one is by far the best that we’ve ever had, and I can say that very truthfully,” Kyle Kirkwood said Friday. “Going by the Capitol building, the views here, all the architecture of all the buildings around here, all the museums, it’s stuff that you dream of. “It’s a serious honor and privilege.”This weekend’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the second big sporting event staged by President Donald Trump in Washington as part of the nation’s 250th birthday celebration. The first was a UFC fight card on the White House’s South Lawn in June.IndyCar racing — an open-wheel counterpart to NASCAR — doesn’t have quite the same association with the right-wing “manosphere” or the MAGA movement, but series owner Roger Penske received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Trump in 2019 and led the effort to put together this race in the District of Columbia.
    
        
    

For the drivers, it’s a welcome moment in the spotlight.“What’s been the coolest part of this week? Honestly, the media covering us,” Kirkwood said. “It’s cool to see IndyCar in this light. We don’t get these opportunities very often outside of the Indy 500, and to have an event that is sought after as much as the 500 is something that’s special.”Washington has little history with high-level motorsports. In 2002, the parking lot at RFK Stadium on the city’s east side was transformed into a course for an American Le Mans Series event.


    
        




    


The Freedom 250 is downtown in one of D.C.'s prime tourist areas. If you’re not in a race car, it’s not the greatest weekend to be driving around the area given all the road closures, but if the weather holds up, the setting has the potential to be spectacular.

“As a boy from the Netherlands that just got his green card, it is really cool,” said Rinus VeeKay, who has six top-10 finishes this season. “We didn’t get too much U.S. history in school ... but learning so much about it here, seeing all the monuments and museums and just how every building kind of has a special purpose here around the city, is very cool. Getting to see the White House, this is stuff you see in movies.”The White House is not part of the D.C. course, although after Turn 1, the track does include a lengthy straightaway along Pennsylvania Avenue, heading northwest away from the Capitol. Then there’s a sharp left turn between the National Archives and the main Justice Department building, followed by a couple quick 90-degree turns as the track navigates the city’s grid system.
    
        
    

After a straightaway takes drivers across the National Mall, they turn left onto Independence Avenue, passing the Smithsonian’s National Air & Space Museum. and the Eisenhower Memorial before heading north on 3rd Street to the finish line, which is just west of the Capitol.“I think it’s more exciting when you actually get on the grounds and see what you’re about to do. I mean, when is this ever going to happen again?” said Josef Newgarden, a driver for Team Penske. “I hope it’s great visibility. That’s probably the biggest thing that it could bring to us — is visibility to people that aren’t maybe as familiar with IndyCar racing.”IndyCar practice and qualifying are scheduled for Saturday, along with an IROC race. The IndyCar race is Sunday and set for 250 miles (147 laps) — the second-longest street circuit race in IndyCar history.
    
        
    

The 1.7-mile track includes seven turns in all. The Air & Space Museum and National Gallery of Art are both inside the course’s perimeter, with a fan zone between them. The track is shorter and has fewer turns than several others on the IndyCar schedule, but it’s not much different from the 1.6-mile, nine-turn circuit used in downtown Detroit.“It’s short and snappy, but you know what? We don’t know. We haven’t driven on it yet,” driver Marcus Armstrong said. “We’ll find out tomorrow. It might even be wet tomorrow. There’s a lot of crosswalks, a lot of paint on the track, so that could be super slippery.”___See AP’s full auto racing coverage here

Art & Culture.title: Kenny Schachter Says Stop Complaining About Art and Do More
Art & Culture.text: Summary'State of Art' is a new HypeArt series inviting artists, curators, collectors and other leading voices to weigh in on the ideas, debates and cultural shifts shaping contemporary art. Through intimate questions and personal recommendations, the series offers a closer look at what is exciting the art world, what needs to change and where things may be heading next.Kenny Schachter has never been easy to categorize, which is largely the point. Artist, writer, curator, lecturer and collector, he has spent more than three decades making work while chronicling, criticizing and occasionally antagonizing the art world around him. His writing has become particularly known for turning insider access into sharp, often self-deprecating commentary on the personalities, money and absurdities driving the contemporary art market.For all the noise Schachter makes around the industry, however, his relationship to art itself remains remarkably earnest.Paul Thek is a case in point. Schachter’s fascination with the late American artist stretches back decades, from collecting his work and contributing to Paul Thek: Artist’s Artist to curating exhibitions dedicated to him, most recently alongside Jonathan Anderson at Thomas Dane Gallery in London in 2025. It’s no surprise, then, that Thek resurfaces throughout Schachter’s answers for our latest State of Art discussion, including a small painting he first encountered in the 1990s and still hasn’t been able to shake. Schachter looks ahead to his own return to the gallery this fall, considers what it takes to keep making when the art world gets gritty and delivers some characteristically succinct advice for anyone spending too much time lamenting its current state: stop complaining and do more. Read our full conversation below.What’s the one show from the first half of this year that you can’t stop thinking about?Paul Thek at Galerie Buchholz in New York City.Did any artwork actually make you feel something real this year, or has everything felt a little flat?No art makes me feel flat. It all moves me, to my marrow, whether good, bad or ugly. Or worse.What did touch me, to the bone, was Paul Thek’s "Bread and Buttocks" (1979–80) at Buchholz, depicting just that: a portion of a male torso and a slice of bread rendered in oil on canvas. The work is small in scale, incorporating a quaint overhanging picture light attached to the antique gold frame and a child’s school chair situated in front to view the diminutive piece. It proves once and for all that size doesn’t matter as much as what you do with it.I first encountered the painting at Thek’s 1995 retrospective, The Wonderful World That Almost Was, in Rotterdam, and subsequently at the Whitney in 2010. I was touched by the colorful composition, play on words and juxtaposition of shards of abstraction with figuration.Though Thek referred to this series as purposefully “bad” in relation to what he saw unfolding in NYC at the time, when artists like Julian Schnabel and Francesco Clemente were painting big and bad — not in a good way — and ruled the roost, I think Thek’s response is f-ing masterful.What’s a show you have marked on your calendar for the rest of the year and why?Not to be (too much of) a pig…but my upcoming show, This Is It, at Alex Berns gallery in New York’s Tribeca in November, where I will present new sculptures, as well as photos and archives from the early 1990s."Every year I am alive, cogent and mobile is a great year for art."If you had to give the 2026 art world a report card grade right now, what is it and why?Every year I am alive, cogent and mobile is a great year for art. The rest of my life is another story, which you’ll be happy to know I won’t get into now.What’s one trend in the art scene you want to see go away and one you want to see more of?Stop complaining and do more.If you could sum up the art world right now in exactly three words, what would they be?Tough. Stay committed. (Or be committed. It might be the easier choice.)If you could grab a drink or meal with any artist tonight, living or dead, who would it be and what’s the first thing you’re asking them?The obvious answer for me is Paul Thek, as I have been obsessed for more than three decades, including curating exhibitions on the artist at Thomas Dane and Pace galleries and writing about him for MIT Press, among other publications.The first thing I would ask is: How did you manage to work so prodigiously and profoundly for so long? Primarily because I’m so damn jealous!Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
